Part 9 of the allocation carried 2 of the 4 ethics marks; because Professional Ethics was left out of Part 10 at the requester's instruction, this file covers the whole Professional Ethics syllabus so the subject is complete in one place.
meta.citation_convention: Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 is cited as 'A&C Act s.X' (as amended in 2015, 2019 and 2021). The Mediation Act 2023 is cited as 'Mediation Act'. The Advocates Act 1961 is cited as 'Advocates Act s.X' and the Bar Council of India Rules, Part VI, Chapter II (Standards of Professional Conduct and Etiquette) as 'BCI Rules'. Evidence provisions use the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA) with the old Evidence Act numbers in brackets.
meta.disclaimer: Prepared as a study aid. Developments after 19 Nov 2026 are not covered. Items tagged [VERIFY] rest on press or secondary reports, or on sub-section and Rule numbers I could not confirm against the bare text (BCI Rule numbers in particular vary in published compilations). Not legal advice.

how_to_use: The 12 marks (4 + 4 + 4) divide evenly across ADR/Arbitration, PIL and Professional Ethics. All three are heavily recall-based and fast to score once the key sections, cases and rules are memorised.

Arbitration: learn the architecture of the A&C Act (Part I, Part II, Part III), then ss.7-9, 11-12, 16-17, 23, 29A, 31, 34, 36-37, 44-48. Time-limits and the 2015/2019/2021 amendments are the favourite targets.

PIL: learn the evolution (Hussainara -> S.P. Gupta -> Bandhua -> Vishaka), the Supreme Court's 1988 categories, the Balwant Singh Chaufal abuse guidelines and the 2026 remarks of the CJI Surya Kant Bench.

Professional Ethics: know the Advocates Act sections (ss.16, 23, 24, 29-35, 36B, 37-38, 49) and the BCI Rules by theme (duty to court, client, opponent, colleagues, other employment). Learn the leading cases on misconduct.

Overlaps: Part 1 (Arts 32, 226, 39A, 21, 129; PIL jurisdiction), Part 2 (compounding, plea bargaining, privileges), Part 3 (CPC s.89, Order X Rules 1A-1C, Order XXIII, Order XXXIIA), Part 7 (arbitration agreement as contract; stamp duty), Part 8 (Consumer mediation; administrative law and PIL), Part 10 (Industrial conciliation; stamp duty).

'Which is NOT ...' - items that are not an advocate's duty or not entertained as PIL

Constitution links: Art 39A, Art 32, Art 226, Art 129

Court's power to modify an award (Gayatri Balasamy, 2025)

s.89 CPC and Commercial Courts Act s.12A (Patil Automation)
PIL: Hussainara, S.P. Gupta, Bandhua Mukti Morcha, Vishaka, Vineet Narain, M.C. Mehta, Balwant Singh Chaufal
Categories not entertained as PIL (1988 Supreme Court guidelines)

time_strategy: Most items are recall; 60 seconds each. Use the open book only to confirm numbers.
For arbitration questions, check whether the subject is Part I (seat in India) or Part II (foreign award).
For ethics, the BCI Rules are often framed as dos and don'ts; if the conduct benefits the client at the cost of honesty to the court, it is almost always misconduct.
common_traps: Section 34 limitation is 3 months, extendable by a maximum of 30 days - not 90 days and not under the Limitation Act s.5.
Patent illegality (s.34(2A)) is available only for domestic awards, not for awards in international commercial arbitration.
An arbitration agreement need not be signed if exchange of communications provides a record (s.7(4)(b)); electronic communication counts.
Lok Adalat awards are decrees but are NOT appealable; challenge is by writ (Bhargavi Constructions).
Permanent Lok Adalats can decide on merits if conciliation fails; ordinary Lok Adalats cannot.
Conciliation settlement has the status of an arbitral award on agreed terms (s.74).
PIL is not available for service matters, landlord-tenant, pension, admissions or early-hearing requests (1988 guidelines).
An advocate cannot have a lien over client papers (R.D. Saxena); but may appropriate unsettled fee from client's money in hand under the BCI Rules.
Only the Bar Council can debar an advocate from practising; the High Court can punish for contempt but cannot take away the licence (Pravin C. Shah).
Appeal against a Bar Council Disciplinary Committee order lies to the Bar Council of India (s.37) and then to the Supreme Court (s.38), each within 60 days.

sections.title: ADR Framework: Negotiation, Mediation, Conciliation, Arbitration, Lok Adalat; Section 89 CPC; Legal Services Authorities Act; Gram Nyayalayas; Family Courts; Commercial Courts s.12A
sections.articles: Art 39A, Art 21; CPC s.89 and Order X Rules 1A-1C; Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 ss.19-22E; Commercial Courts Act 2015 s.12A; Family Courts Act 1984; Gram Nyayalayas Act 2008
sections.overview: The map of dispute-resolution methods and the statutory institutions around them. Know who decides, whether the outcome is binding, and which statute governs.
must_know: ADR methods: (1) Negotiation - direct, voluntary; no third party. (2) Mediation - neutral facilitator helps parties reach a voluntary settlement; mediator does not decide. (3) Conciliation - conciliator may propose settlement terms (A&C Act Part III). (4) Arbitration - private adjudication by a tribunal chosen by parties; award binding. (5) Lok Adalat - statutory people's court; settlement by compromise; award is a civil-court decree. (6) Judicial settlement, med-arb, early neutral evaluation, mini-trial, Online Dispute Resolution (ODR). Benefits: speed, cost, confidentiality, preserving relationships, reducing docket; constitutional anchor: Art 39A (equal justice and free legal aid) and Art 21 (speedy justice).

Section 89 CPC and Order X Rules 1A, 1B, 1C: where it appears to the court that there exist elements of a settlement which may be acceptable to the parties, the court shall formulate the terms of settlement and refer the same for (a) arbitration; (b) conciliation; (c) judicial settlement including settlement through Lok Adalat; or (d) mediation. Salem Advocate Bar Association v. Union of India (2005): validity upheld; court to follow Rules; Afcons Infrastructure Ltd. v. Cherian Varkey Construction Co. (2010): the court cannot refer parties to arbitration without the consent of both sides (arbitration needs agreement); mandatory referral to Lok Adalat, conciliation, mediation allowed without consent as steps; categories of cases generally unsuitable for ADR: representative suits (Order I Rule 8), election disputes, grant of probate/letters of administration, cases involving public interest and serious allegations of fraud, cases against minors/persons of unsound mind, prosecution for criminal offences; suited: relating to trade, commerce, contracts, specific performance, motor accident claims (some), partition, matrimonial, family disputes, consumer, banking etc. Order XXIII Rule 3 CPC: compromise decree. Order XXXIIA: family matters - conciliation.

Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 (in force 9 November 1995; 'National Legal Services Day'): Art 39A. NALSA (apex body; Chief Justice of India is Patron-in-Chief; an executive chairman who is a serving/retired Supreme Court judge); State Legal Services Authority (Chief Justice of the High Court is Patron-in-Chief), District Legal Services Authority (District Judge is Chairman), Taluk Legal Services Committee, High Court Legal Services Committee, Supreme Court Legal Services Committee. Persons entitled to free legal services (s.12): members of Scheduled Castes/Tribes; victim of trafficking or begar; women and children; persons with disabilities; persons in circumstances of undeserved want such as victims of mass disaster, ethnic violence, caste atrocity, flood, drought, earthquake or industrial disaster; industrial workmen; persons in custody (including protective home, juvenile home, psychiatric hospital); persons whose annual income is below the limit fixed by the Government (for Supreme Court cases, Rs 5 lakh as notified).

Lok Adalat (Chapter VI, ss.19-22 LSA Act): organised by the Authorities at periodic intervals; consists of serving or retired judicial officers and other persons as prescribed; jurisdiction over (i) any case pending before any court; or (ii) any matter falling within the jurisdiction of any court and not brought before it (pre-litigation) - but no jurisdiction over any offence not compoundable under the law (s.19(5)). Cases are referred if (i) the parties agree, or one party applies and the court is prima facie satisfied that there are chances of settlement (s.20); the Lok Adalat shall proceed in a summary manner guided by principles of justice, equity, fair play and other principles (s.20(4)); where no compromise is reached the record is returned to the court for disposal in accordance with law (s.20(5)). Award (s.21): deemed a decree of a civil court; final and binding on all parties; no appeal lies; court fee paid is refunded under the Court Fees Act. Powers (s.22): same as a civil court for summoning and examining witnesses, discovery and production of documents, receiving evidence on affidavits, requisitioning public records; proceedings are judicial proceedings for ss.193, 219, 228 IPC (BNS equivalents) and a civil court for s.195 CrPC (s.215 BNSS). National Lok Adalats are held on specified dates; special Lok Adalats for specific subjects (e.g., motor accident claims, bank recovery, electricity, matrimonial).

Lok Adalat jurisprudence: State of Punjab v. Jalour Singh (2008) - a Lok Adalat has no adjudicatory role; it can only help parties arrive at a compromise by consent; an award made without consent is a nullity; P.T. Thomas v. Thomas Job (2005) - the Lok Adalat award has the finality of a decree and cannot be challenged except on very limited grounds; Bhargavi Constructions v. Kothakapu Muthyam Reddy (2018) - an award can be challenged only by a writ petition under Arts 226/227 on grounds such as fraud or coercion (no appeal; no civil suit); B.P. Moideen Sevamandir v. A.M. Kutty Hassan (2009) - the Lok Adalat is not a 'court' for deciding merits; K.N. Govindan Kutty Menon v. C.D. Shaji (2012): Lok Adalat award can be challenged only by writ.

Permanent Lok Adalats (ss.22A-22E, inserted by the 2002 Amendment) - for public utility services: transport services for carriage of passengers or goods by air, road or water; postal, telegraph or telephone services; supply of power, light or water to the public by any establishment; public conservancy or sanitation; services in hospitals or dispensaries; insurance services; and (by notification) education or other public utility services. Composition: Chairman who is or has been a District Judge/Additional District Judge or has held higher judicial office, and two members with adequate experience in public utility services. Jurisdiction: pre-litigation only (a party must not have approached a court) over disputes involving public utility services where the value of the property in dispute does not exceed Rs 1 crore (raised from Rs 10 lakh by 2015 notification [VERIFY]); excludes non-compoundable offences. Procedure (s.22C): conciliation first; if no settlement the PLA has the power to decide the dispute on merits (unlike ordinary Lok Adalats); the award is final, binding and a decree (s.22E); no appeal. United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Ajay Sinha (2008): PLA's adjudicatory role upheld; the pre-litigation settlement process must be strictly followed.

Gram Nyayalayas Act 2008 (in force 2 October 2009): village courts established at the intermediate Panchayat level by the State Government in consultation with the High Court; presided by a Nyayadhikari (a judicial officer with powers of a Judicial Magistrate First Class); mobile court sittings at village level; civil and criminal jurisdiction as per Schedules; emphasis on conciliation; simplified procedure; appeals - criminal: to the Court of Session (within 30 days; to be disposed within six months), civil: to the District Court (within 30 days; to be disposed within six months) [VERIFY]; number actually operational is limited [VERIFY].

Family Courts Act 1984: Family Courts established for settlement of matrimonial and family disputes; s.9 - duty of the court to make efforts for settlement and to assist and persuade parties; s.13 - no party has a right to be represented by a legal practitioner (court may appoint amicus curiae); s.10 - procedure; s.19 - appeal to the High Court within 30 days; mediation in matrimonial cases: K. Srinivas Rao v. D.A. Deepa (2013) - directions on mediation in cruelty cases (including s.498A IPC / s.85 BNS) and sending matters to mediation; Hindu Marriage Act s.23(2) - reconciliation. [Cross-ref Part 6.]

Commercial Courts Act 2015, s.12A (inserted 2018): a suit which does not contemplate any urgent interim relief shall not be instituted unless the plaintiff exhausts the remedy of pre-institution mediation in accordance with the Commercial Courts (Pre-Institution Mediation and Settlement) Rules 2018; commercial disputes of 'specified value' (Rs 3 lakh and above). Patil Automation Pvt. Ltd. v. Rakheja Engineers Pvt. Ltd. (2022): s.12A is mandatory; plaint is liable to be rejected under Order VII Rule 11(d) CPC; applied prospectively from 20 August 2022; Yamini Manohar v. T.K.D. Keerthi (2023): the court must assess whether 'urgent interim relief' is genuine and not a cover to avoid mediation. Mediation under the Rules must be completed within three months (extendable by two months with consent); settlement agreement has the same status as an arbitral award on agreed terms (s.12A(5)).

Other ADR institutions and statutes: Consumer Protection Act 2019 - reference to mediation (s.37) and mediation cells (ss.74-81) [VERIFY]; Industrial Disputes Act/IR Code - conciliation officers and voluntary arbitration; Banking Ombudsman Scheme (now the Reserve Bank - Integrated Ombudsman Scheme 2021); Insurance Ombudsman Rules 2017; SEBI Online Dispute Resolution portal (2023); Online Dispute Resolution Policy Plan for India (NITI Aayog, 2021); MCA-21 'Company Law Settlement'; Panchayat Nyaya; Tribal customary dispute mechanisms; Supreme Court Mediation and Conciliation Project Committee (MCPC) - 'Mediation for the Nation' campaign launched in July 2025 for pending matters [VERIFY].

key_provisions.content: Court-referred settlement: arbitration, conciliation, judicial settlement (Lok Adalat), mediation.
Lok Adalat award: deemed decree; final and binding; no appeal.
Permanent Lok Adalat may decide on merits if conciliation fails.
Mandatory pre-institution mediation unless urgent interim relief is contemplated.
Settlement efforts; no right of legal representation.

sections.title: Mediation and Conciliation: Mediation Act 2023, Mediation Council of India, Singapore Convention and Part III of the A&C Act 1996
sections.articles: Mediation Act 2023; A&C Act Part III (ss.61-81)
sections.overview: India now has a standalone mediation statute and a statutory regulator. Conciliation under Part III of the 1996 Act remains in place. Questions test definitions, enforceability and who may challenge a settlement.
must_know: Mediation Act 2023: received Presidential assent on 14 September 2023; some provisions (including those on the Mediation Council) were brought into force on 9 October 2023 [VERIFY the status of the remaining provisions]. Eight Chapters and two Schedules (about 62 sections). Purpose: to promote, encourage and facilitate mediation (especially institutional mediation) for commercial and other disputes; enforce mediated settlement agreements; provide for community mediation; make online mediation legal; provide for a body for registration of mediators; and give effect to the Singapore Convention on Mediation.

Definition: 'mediation' - a process, whether referred to as mediation, pre-litigation mediation, online mediation, community mediation, conciliation or an expression of similar import, whereby parties to a dispute, with the assistance of a third person (the mediator), attempt to reach an amicable settlement. The mediator facilitates; he does not impose a settlement.

Applicability: (a) mediation conducted in India where all or both parties habitually reside in or are incorporated or have their place of business in India; (b) international mediation (commercial; at least one party is a foreign national, foreign resident or foreign-incorporated entity; mediation conducted in India); (c) mediation agreements providing for mediation under the Act; (d) disputes to which the Central or State Government is party, only commercial disputes. Disputes unfit for mediation are listed in the First Schedule - for example, disputes involving criminal prosecution or non-compoundable offences, claims affecting rights of minors or persons of unsound mind, matters affecting the rights of third parties, and tax matters [VERIFY list].

Pre-litigation mediation: before filing any civil or commercial suit or proceeding, parties may, by mutual consent (the Act makes this voluntary rather than compulsory [VERIFY]), refer the dispute to mediation; a party may withdraw after two mediation sessions; a court may refer the parties to mediation at any stage (cf. s.89 CPC). Mediation is to be completed within 120 days from the first appearance before the mediator, extendable by 60 days with consent [VERIFY]. Mediators are subject to disclosure and impartiality duties; confidentiality of mediation communications is protected; communications and proposals made in mediation are privileged and not admissible in other proceedings.

Mediated Settlement Agreement (MSA): written, signed by parties and authenticated by the mediator; final and binding on the parties and enforceable as if it were a judgment or decree of the court; may be registered with the Legal Services Authority (State/District) within 90 days; MSA arising from pre-litigation mediation has the status of a decree; an MSA can be challenged only on grounds of fraud, corruption, impersonation or because the dispute was not fit for mediation, within 90 days of receipt of the MSA (extendable by a further 90 days) [VERIFY periods].

Mediation Council of India: a statutory body to promote and regulate mediation - registration of mediators; recognition of mediation service providers and institutes; maintaining a repository; setting standards; the Central Government notified the establishment of the Council (August 2026 - reported 27 August 2026 [VERIFY]), after a Parliamentary panel's urging. Community mediation: for disputes likely to affect peace and harmony among residents of a locality; Community Mediation Panel of three mediators. Online mediation allowed; international mediation covered; Singapore Convention on Mediation (United Nations Convention on International Settlement Agreements Resulting from Mediation): adopted December 2018; signing ceremony 7 August 2019 (India among the signatories); in force from 12 September 2020; ratification by India is awaited [VERIFY].

Court-annexed mediation: Supreme Court's Mediation and Conciliation Project Committee (MCPC); Civil Procedure ADR and Mediation Rules 2003 (Salem Advocate Bar Association); mediation in matrimonial and commercial disputes; mediators trained; confidential; settlement is recorded as a decree under Order XXIII Rule 3 CPC.

Conciliation under Part III of the A&C Act 1996 (ss.61-81), based on the UNCITRAL Conciliation Rules 1980: s.61 - applies to conciliation of disputes arising out of a legal relationship, contractual or not, and to proceedings relating thereto (not to disputes that by law cannot be submitted to conciliation). s.62 - commencement: by one party sending a written invitation to the other; conciliation begins when the other accepts in writing; if the invitation is not accepted within 30 days it is treated as rejected. s.63 - one conciliator unless parties agree on two or three; s.64 - appointment (each party appoints one when two; third as presiding conciliator). s.65 - statements to conciliator; s.66 - conciliator is not bound by the CPC or the Evidence Act; s.67 - role: assist parties in an independent and impartial manner; guided by principles of objectivity, fairness and justice, trade usage and the circumstances; may conduct proceedings as he considers appropriate and may make proposals for settlement at any stage. s.69 - communication; s.70 - disclosure of information; s.72 - suggestions by parties for settlement; s.73 - settlement agreement: when it appears to the conciliator that there exist elements of a settlement, he formulates the terms and submits them to the parties; if parties agree they draw up and sign a settlement agreement; the conciliator may authenticate it; s.74 - status and effect: the settlement agreement has the same status and effect as if it were an arbitral award on agreed terms under s.30 (so it is enforceable as a decree - s.36); s.75 - confidentiality; s.76 - termination of conciliation (by settlement agreement; by written declaration of conciliator that further efforts are no longer justified; by written declaration of parties; by written declaration of a party); s.77 - no arbitral or judicial proceedings in respect of the dispute while conciliation is on, except to preserve rights; s.80 - the conciliator shall not act as an arbitrator or as a representative or counsel of a party in any arbitral or judicial proceeding in respect of the same dispute; s.81 - admissions, views, suggestions, proposals made in conciliation are not admissible in other proceedings.

Conciliation v. mediation v. arbitration: conciliator may propose terms and the settlement has the status of an award (s.74); mediator facilitates (Mediation Act); arbitrator decides and binds. Statutory conciliation also exists in labour law (Industrial Disputes Act / IR Code) and in the Family Courts Act (s.9).

Relationship with arbitration: parties may agree to 'med-arb' - mediation followed by arbitration; the arbitral tribunal may encourage settlement (s.30 A&C Act) - the tribunal may use mediation, conciliation or other procedures at any time; settlement terms may be recorded as an arbitral award on agreed terms (s.30(4)), having the same status as any other award.

No arbitral/judicial proceedings during conciliation, except to preserve rights.
Conciliator cannot act as arbitrator or counsel; conciliation communications inadmissible elsewhere.
Statutory framework; MSA enforceable as a decree; Mediation Council of India.

sections.articles: A&C Act ss.2-11, 20, 42; Part II; Schedules
sections.overview: The architecture of the Act, what makes an arbitration agreement, when a court must send parties to arbitration, how arbitrators are appointed, arbitrability and the seat-venue distinction.
must_know: Scheme: Part I (ss.2-43) - domestic arbitration and international commercial arbitration held in India (the 'seat' in India); Part IA (ss.43A-43M) - Arbitration Council of India (inserted 2019; never operationalised) [VERIFY current status]; Part II (ss.44-60) - enforcement of certain foreign awards: Chapter I - New York Convention awards (ss.44-52), Chapter II - Geneva Convention awards (ss.53-60); Part III (ss.61-81) - conciliation; Part IV (ss.82-86) - supplementary provisions. Schedules: First (New York Convention), Second (Geneva Protocol 1923), Third (Geneva Convention 1927), Fourth (model fee schedule; 2015), Fifth (grounds giving rise to justifiable doubts as to independence or impartiality; 2015), Sixth (disclosure form), Seventh (persons ineligible to be arbitrators); the Eighth Schedule (qualifications of arbitrators, 2019) was omitted by the 2021 Amendment. Based on the UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration 1985 and the UNCITRAL Conciliation Rules 1980; the Act replaced the Arbitration Act 1940, the Arbitration (Protocol and Convention) Act 1937 and the Foreign Awards (Recognition and Enforcement) Act 1961.

Amendments: Arbitration and Conciliation (Amendment) Act 2015 (effective 23 October 2015) - 'public policy' narrowed; patent illegality (s.34(2A)); time-limits (s.29A, s.23(4)); s.9 interim relief safeguards; s.11 reforms; Schedules; costs (s.31A); BCCI v. Kochi Cricket Pvt. Ltd. (2018) - the 2015 Amendment applies prospectively to arbitral proceedings commenced on or after 23 Oct 2015 and to court proceedings in relation to them (not to s.34 applications pending on that date). 2019 Amendment - arbitral institutions designation (s.11(3A)), s.23(4), s.29A revisions, Part IA (ACI), confidentiality (s.42A), immunity (s.42B). 2021 Amendment (Act 3 of 2021) - unconditional stay on enforcement of an award if the underlying agreement or award was induced by fraud or corruption (proviso to s.36(3)); omission of the Eighth Schedule. Draft Arbitration and Conciliation (Amendment) Bill 2024 (based on the Expert Committee headed by Dr T.K. Viswanathan, Feb 2024) was circulated for comments but had not been enacted as of November 2026 [VERIFY].

Definitions (s.2(1)): 'arbitration' - any arbitration whether or not administered by a permanent arbitral institution; 'arbitral award' includes an interim award; 'Court' (s.2(1)(e)) - for domestic arbitration the principal civil court of original jurisdiction in a district (including the High Court in the exercise of ordinary original civil jurisdiction) having jurisdiction to decide the subject-matter if it were the subject of a suit, but not a Small Cause Court; for international commercial arbitration the High Court (original jurisdiction or having appellate jurisdiction). 'International commercial arbitration' (s.2(1)(f)) - arbitration relating to disputes arising out of legal relationships, contractual or not, considered commercial under Indian law, where at least one party is (i) an individual who is a national of, or habitually resident in, any country other than India; (ii) a body corporate incorporated outside India; (iii) a company, association or body of individuals whose central management and control is exercised in any country other than India; or (iv) the Government of a foreign country.

Scope (s.2(2)): Part I applies where the place (seat) of arbitration is in India; ss.9, 27, 37(1)(a) and 37(3) apply to international commercial arbitration even if the seat is outside India (unless parties agree otherwise), provided the award is enforceable under Part II. Bharat Aluminium Co. v. Kaiser Aluminium Technical Services (BALCO, 2012, Constitution Bench): Part I applies only to arbitrations seated in India; it overruled Bhatia International v. Bulk Trading S.A. (2002) and Venture Global Engineering v. Satyam Computers (2008); the decision applies prospectively to arbitration agreements executed after 6 September 2012. s.5 - extent of judicial intervention: no judicial authority shall intervene except where so provided in Part I; s.6 - administrative assistance.

Arbitration agreement (s.7): an agreement by the parties to submit to arbitration all or certain disputes which have arisen or may arise in respect of a defined legal relationship, contractual or not; may be a clause in a contract or a separate agreement; must be in writing; written if contained in (a) a document signed by the parties; (b) an exchange of letters, telex, telegrams or other means of telecommunication (including electronic communication) providing a record of the agreement; or (c) an exchange of statements of claim and defence in which the existence of the agreement is alleged by one party and not denied by the other; a reference in a contract to a document containing an arbitration clause constitutes an arbitration agreement if the reference makes that clause part of the contract (s.7(5)). Essentials (K.K. Modi v. K.N. Modi, 1998; Jagdish Chander v. Ramesh Chander, 2007): agreement to refer disputes; binding decision; tribunal's jurisdiction from consent; no mere right to consult; words like 'may' are not conclusive. Separability (s.16(1)(b)): an arbitration clause is independent of the contract; termination or invalidity of the contract does not invalidate the clause (Enercon (India) Ltd. v. Enercon GmbH, 2014). Incorporation by reference: M.R. Engineers v. Som Datt Builders (2009); Inox Wind Ltd. v. Thermocables Ltd. (2018); Duro Felguera S.A. v. Gangavaram Port Ltd. (2017) - s.11 court looks only at existence of the agreement.

Reference to arbitration (s.8): a judicial authority before which an action is brought in a matter which is the subject of an arbitration agreement shall, if a party applies not later than the date of submitting his first statement on the substance of the dispute, refer the parties to arbitration unless it finds that prima facie no valid arbitration agreement exists (2015); the application must be accompanied by the original agreement or a certified copy; arbitration may commence and an award may be made while the application is pending. Sukanya Holdings Pvt. Ltd. v. Jayesh H. Pandya (2003): s.8 does not apply where the suit includes parties or subject-matter not covered by the agreement; Booz Allen & Hamilton v. SBI Home Finance (2011): disputes relating to rights in rem (e.g., mortgage enforcement) are not arbitrable; A. Ayyasamy v. A. Paramasivam (2016) and Rashid Raza v. Sadaf Akhtar (2019) on fraud; Avitel Post Studioz Ltd. v. HSBC PI Holdings (2020): allegations of fraud do not by themselves bar arbitration unless they are of a nature affecting the public or relate to rights in rem.

Arbitrability and the scope of court scrutiny: Vidya Drolia v. Durga Trading Corporation (2020, three judges): a four-fold test for non-arbitrability - disputes (i) relating to actions in rem that do not pertain to subordinate rights in personam; (ii) affecting third-party rights, requiring centralised adjudication; (iii) relating to inalienable sovereign and public interest functions of the State; (iv) expressly or by necessary implication non-arbitrable under a statute; landlord-tenant disputes governed by the Transfer of Property Act are arbitrable, but eviction under special rent statutes is not; courts at the referral stage apply a 'prima facie' test and refuse only where the claim is 'ex facie' non-arbitrable ('eyes wide shut' approach); the arbitral tribunal decides arbitrability (competence-competence). In re: Interplay between Arbitration Agreements under the A&C Act 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act 1899 (13 Dec 2023, seven judges): an unstamped arbitration agreement is not void but inadmissible; the defect is curable; the court at the s.11 stage does not examine stamping; the tribunal does. Cox and Kings Ltd. v. SAP India Pvt. Ltd. (6 Dec 2023, Constitution Bench): the 'group of companies' doctrine is part of Indian arbitration law - a non-signatory may be bound by an arbitration agreement on the basis of the parties' mutual intention, conduct, composite transactions and the commercial reality; the tribunal examines whether a non-signatory is a 'veritable party'; the court's s.11 inquiry is prima facie.

Interim measures by court (s.9): a party may apply to a court before, during or after arbitral proceedings (but before enforcement under s.36) for interim measures such as preservation of goods, injunction, appointment of receiver, security for the amount in dispute, interim custody; if the court grants interim measure before the commencement of arbitral proceedings, the proceedings must be commenced within 90 days (or such further time as the court allows) (s.9(2)); once the tribunal is constituted, the court shall not entertain a s.9 application unless it finds that the remedy under s.17 is not efficacious (s.9(3)); Arcelor Mittal Nippon Steel India Ltd. v. Essar Bulk Terminal Ltd. (2021) - Order XXXVIII Rule 5 CPC principles are not strictly applicable; the court must consider the broad principles of interim relief; Amazon.com NV Investment Holdings v. Future Retail Ltd. (2021) - an emergency arbitrator's interim award under institutional rules is an 'order' of the tribunal under s.17(1) enforceable under s.17(2). Applies in ICA with a foreign seat (s.2(2) proviso).

Appointment of arbitrators (ss.10-11): number must not be even (s.10); default is a sole arbitrator; for three arbitrators each party appoints one and the two appoint the presiding arbitrator (s.11(3)); if a party fails to appoint within 30 days of receipt of a request, or the two appointed arbitrators fail to agree on the third within 30 days (s.11(4)), the appointment is made on request by the Supreme Court or High Court or by any person or institution designated by it (s.11(6) etc.); s.11(5) - sole arbitrator default; s.11(6) - failure of appointment procedure; s.11(6A) (2015) - the Court shall confine itself to the examination of the existence of an arbitration agreement (the 2019 Amendment omitted s.11(6A), but the Supreme Court continues to apply a prima facie, minimal-scrutiny approach: Mayavati Trading Pvt. Ltd. v. Pradyuat Deb Burman, 2019; Vidya Drolia; In re Interplay) [VERIFY]; s.11(12) - in international commercial arbitration the Supreme Court (or its designate) appoints; in domestic arbitration the High Court; s.11(13) - the application shall be disposed of expeditiously and endeavour made to dispose of within 60 days from service of notice on the opposite party; s.11(14) - fee fixed per the Fourth Schedule. s.11(3A)-(3B) (2019): the Supreme Court and High Courts shall designate arbitral institutions graded by the Arbitration Council of India; the ACI has not been constituted, so appointments continue to be made by courts.

Seat and venue: place of arbitration (s.20) - parties are free to agree on the place; failing agreement the tribunal determines it having regard to convenience; the tribunal may meet at any place for consultation, hearing witnesses or inspection. Seat = the legal place determining the lex arbitri and the supervisory court; Indus Mobile Distribution Pvt. Ltd. v. Datawind Innovations (2017): once the seat is designated, the courts of the seat have exclusive jurisdiction notwithstanding contrary clauses; Union of India v. Hardy Exploration and Production (India) Inc. (2018) and BGS SGS SOMA JV v. NHPC Ltd. (2019): where the agreement designates a 'venue' without any contrary indicium, the venue is the seat; Mankastu Impex Pvt. Ltd. v. Airvisual Ltd. (2020). Jurisdiction (s.42): where any application has been made in a court under Part I with respect to an arbitration agreement, that court alone has jurisdiction over the arbitral proceedings and all subsequent applications (State of West Bengal v. Associated Contractors, 2015).

sections.title: Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 (II): Independence of Arbitrators, Tribunal's Jurisdiction, Interim Measures, Procedure, Time-limits, Award, Costs and Interest
sections.overview: How a tribunal is kept independent, how it rules on its own jurisdiction, procedure and the strict time-limits, and what a valid award must contain.
must_know: Disclosure and grounds of challenge (s.12): a person approached for appointment shall disclose in writing any circumstances (financial, business, professional, personal) likely to give rise to justifiable doubts as to independence or impartiality and likely to affect his ability to devote sufficient time (s.12(1)); the Sixth Schedule gives the disclosure form; the Fifth Schedule lists grounds giving rise to justifiable doubts (for example, relationship with a party or counsel; previous involvement; direct or indirect interest in the dispute; being a lawyer in the same law firm as the counsel); s.12(3) - an arbitrator may be challenged only if circumstances give rise to justifiable doubts as to his independence or impartiality or he does not possess the qualifications agreed by the parties; s.12(5) - notwithstanding any prior agreement, a person whose relationship with the parties, counsel or the subject-matter falls under any category of the Seventh Schedule is ineligible to be appointed (examples: employee, consultant or advisor of a party; manager/director/part of the management of a party; a person who regularly advises a party; person with a significant financial relationship); this ineligibility can be waived only by an express written agreement made after disputes have arisen (proviso to s.12(5)).

Case law on independence: TRF Ltd. v. Energo Engineering Projects Ltd. (2017) - a person who is ineligible under the Seventh Schedule cannot nominate another arbitrator (de jure inability); Voestalpine Schienen GmbH v. Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (2017) - independence and impartiality of arbitrators in public contracts; Perkins Eastman Architects DPC v. HSCC (India) Ltd. (2019) - unilateral appointment of a sole arbitrator by one party is invalid; Bharat Broadband Network Ltd. v. United Telecoms Ltd. (2019) - waiver under proviso to s.12(5) only by express agreement in writing; Central Organisation for Railway Electrification v. ECI-SPIC-SMO-MCML (JV) (Nov 2024, Constitution Bench) - the principle of equal treatment of parties applies to the appointment stage; clauses allowing one party to unilaterally appoint, or to nominate from a panel it controls, violate equal treatment (applied prospectively) [VERIFY details]; HRD Corporation (Marcus Oil and Chemical Division) v. Gail (India) Ltd. (2017) - arbitrator's bias test.

Challenge procedure (s.13): parties are free to agree; failing agreement, a party who intends to challenge sends a written statement of reasons to the tribunal within 15 days after becoming aware of the constitution of the tribunal or of the circumstances; if the challenged arbitrator does not withdraw and the other party does not agree, the tribunal decides; if the challenge is unsuccessful the tribunal continues and makes the award; the challenging party may apply to set aside the award under s.34. Termination of mandate (ss.14-15): when an arbitrator becomes de jure or de facto unable to perform his functions or fails to act without undue delay, his mandate terminates if he withdraws or the parties agree; otherwise a party may apply to the court; mandate also terminates on withdrawal, by agreement of the parties, or on delay (s.29A). Substitute arbitrator is appointed under the same rules (s.15(2)); the tribunal decides whether previous hearings are to be repeated (s.15(3)).

Competence-competence (s.16): the arbitral tribunal may rule on its own jurisdiction, including ruling on any objection with respect to the existence or validity of the arbitration agreement; the arbitration clause is treated as an agreement independent of the other terms of the contract; a decision that the contract is null and void does not entail ipso jure invalidity of the arbitration clause. A plea that the tribunal does not have jurisdiction shall be raised not later than the submission of the statement of defence; a plea that the tribunal is exceeding the scope of its authority shall be raised as soon as the matter alleged to be beyond the scope is raised during the proceedings; the tribunal may admit a later plea if it considers the delay justified (s.16(2)-(4)). If the tribunal rules that it has jurisdiction, it continues with the arbitration and makes an award; a party aggrieved can challenge the award under s.34 (s.16(5)-(6)); if the tribunal accepts the plea of no jurisdiction an appeal lies under s.37(2)(a). The doctrine was reaffirmed in SBP & Co. v. Patel Engineering (2005) (later overruled in part by the 2015 Amendment as to the nature of the court's role at s.11) and Vidya Drolia (2020).

Interim measures by the tribunal (s.17): during the arbitral proceedings (or after the award but before enforcement - 2015) a party may apply for orders such as preservation of goods, security for amount in dispute, interim injunction, appointment of receiver; the tribunal's order is deemed an order of the court and is enforceable as if it were an order of the court under the CPC (s.17(2)). s.18 - equal treatment: parties shall be treated with equality and each party shall be given a full opportunity to present his case. s.19 - the tribunal is not bound by the CPC or the Indian Evidence Act (BSA); parties may agree on the procedure; failing agreement the tribunal conducts proceedings as it considers appropriate; determines admissibility, relevance, materiality and weight of evidence. s.21 - commencement of arbitral proceedings: on the date on which a request for the dispute to be referred to arbitration is received by the respondent; s.22 - language; s.23 - statements of claim and defence (to be completed within six months from the date the arbitrator(s) receive notice of appointment - s.23(4), 2019); counter-claim and set-off (s.23(2A), 2015); s.24 - hearings: oral hearings as the tribunal decides; the tribunal shall, as far as possible, hold oral hearings for presentation of evidence or oral argument on day-to-day basis and shall not grant any adjournments unless sufficient cause is made out; may impose costs for adjournments; s.25 - default of a party (claimant's default: terminate proceedings; respondent's default: continue; not treated as admission); s.26 - expert appointed by tribunal; s.27 - court assistance in taking evidence (the tribunal or a party with the approval of the tribunal may apply to the court; court may order a person to give evidence; the person failing is subject to penalties and punishments by the court).

Applicable law and award on the merits (s.28): in domestic arbitration (place in India) the tribunal decides in accordance with the substantive law in force in India; in international commercial arbitration, in accordance with the rules of law designated by the parties (any designation of the law of a country refers to the substantive law and not the conflict-of-law rules); failing designation, the rules of law the tribunal considers appropriate; tribunal decides ex aequo et bono or as amiable compositeur only if the parties expressly authorise; in all cases the tribunal decides in accordance with the terms of the contract and takes into account the usages of the trade (s.28(3)); a tribunal shall not decide against the terms of the contract (2015; Associate Builders). s.29 - decision by majority; the presiding arbitrator may decide procedural questions if authorised by the parties or all members; s.30 - settlement: the tribunal may use mediation, conciliation or other procedures to encourage settlement (with the parties' agreement); if the parties settle, the tribunal terminates the proceedings and, if requested, records the settlement as an arbitral award on agreed terms, which has the same status as any other award (s.30(4)).

Time-limits for completing arbitration - s.29A (2015, substantially revised in 2019): in matters other than international commercial arbitration the award must be made within 12 months from the date of completion of pleadings under s.23(4) (the pleadings must themselves be completed within six months); if the award is made within six months from the date the tribunal enters upon the reference the tribunal is entitled to additional fee as agreed; the parties may by consent extend the period by up to six months; if the award is not made within the period (including the extended period) the mandate terminates unless the court, on application of any party and for sufficient cause, extends the period (before or after expiry); on extension the court may reduce the arbitrators' fees by up to five per cent for each month of delay attributable to the tribunal and may substitute one or all of the arbitrators; proceedings continue from the stage already reached; the court may impose actual or exemplary costs on a party; the application under s.29A is to be disposed of within 60 days from service of notice on the opposite party (s.29A(9)). The ICA is not covered by the 12-month rule (the tribunal 'may endeavour' to complete within 12 months). s.29B (2015) - fast-track procedure: parties may agree in writing to resolve disputes by a sole arbitrator on the basis of written pleadings, documents and submissions, with no oral hearing unless requested or considered necessary, and with the award within six months of the tribunal entering upon the reference.

Form and contents of award (s.31): in writing and signed by the members of the tribunal (signatures of the majority suffice if the reason for any omitted signature is stated); shall state reasons upon which it is based unless the parties have agreed that no reasons are to be given or it is an award on agreed terms under s.30; shall state its date and the place of arbitration; a signed copy shall be delivered to each party. Interest (s.31(7)): unless otherwise agreed, where the award is for payment of money the tribunal may include interest on the sum for the whole or any part of the period between the date on which the cause of action arose and the date of the award; a sum directed to be paid by the award carries interest at 2% higher than the current rate of interest prevailing on the date of the award from the date of the award to the date of payment (unless the award directs otherwise) (s.31(7)(b)); 'current rate of interest' as defined in s.2(b) of the Interest Act 1978. Costs (s.31A, 2015): the court or tribunal has discretion to determine whether costs are payable, the amount and when; the general rule is that costs follow the event (the unsuccessful party pays), with deviation for reasons recorded; relevant circumstances include conduct of the parties, whether a party has succeeded partly, any admissible offer to settle. Partial and interim awards (s.31(6)). s.32 - termination of proceedings by the final award or by order of the tribunal (claimant withdraws; parties agree; continuation becomes unnecessary or impossible); mandate terminates with the termination of proceedings subject to ss.33 and 34(4). s.33 - correction and interpretation: within 30 days of receipt of the award (unless another period agreed) a party with notice to the other may request correction of computational, clerical or typographical errors or errors of similar nature, or interpretation of a specific point; additional award on claims presented but omitted may be requested within 30 days; the tribunal makes corrections within 30 days and additional award within 60 days.

Fees and deposits (ss.38-39): the Fourth Schedule gives a model fee scale (maximum fee Rs 30 lakh for a sole arbitrator plus); ONGC Ltd. v. Afcons Gunanusa JV (2022) - fees of arbitrators in public sector contracts; s.38 - deposits as advance for costs; s.39 - lien of the arbitral tribunal on the award for unpaid costs (the court may order the delivery of the award on payment into court). s.40 - arbitration agreement is not discharged by the death of a party; s.41 - provisions as to insolvency.

Confidentiality and immunity (2019): s.42A - the arbitrator, the arbitral institution and the parties shall maintain confidentiality of all arbitral proceedings except the award where its disclosure is necessary for implementation and enforcement; s.42B - no suit or legal proceedings against an arbitrator for anything done or intended to be done in good faith under the Act. Section 43 - Limitation Act 1963 applies to arbitrations as it applies to proceedings in court; arbitration is deemed to commence on the date referred to in s.21; where an award is set aside the time between the commencement of arbitration and the date of the order of the court is excluded for the purposes of limitation for fresh arbitration (s.43(4)).

Statutory arbitration: s.2(4) - Part I applies to every arbitration under any other enactment in force, except in so far as inconsistent; s.2(5) - the Act applies to arbitration agreed under special enactments with exceptions; e.g., arbitration under the Industrial Disputes Act (voluntary arbitration), Cooperative Societies Acts, MSMED Act 2006 (ss.15-24 - Micro and Small Enterprises Facilitation Council; the Supreme Court in Gujarat State Civil Supplies Corporation v. Mahakali Foods (2022) held that MSMED Act arbitration is statutory and that s.18 prevails over s.8 A&C Act; the facilitation council may itself act as arbitrator or refer the dispute to an institution).

sections.title: Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 (III): Setting Aside, Enforcement, Appeals, Public Policy, Modification of Awards; Foreign Awards (Part II); Institutional Arbitration
sections.articles: A&C Act ss.34-37, 42-43; Part II ss.44-60
sections.overview: The grounds and limits of challenge, the 2015 narrowing of public policy, Gayatri Balasamy (2025) on limited modification, how awards are enforced, and recognition of foreign awards.
must_know: Setting aside (s.34): recourse to a court against an arbitral award is only by an application for setting aside. Grounds (s.34(2)(a)) - to be proved by the applicant: (i) a party was under some incapacity; (ii) the arbitration agreement is not valid under the law to which the parties have subjected it; (iii) the applicant was not given proper notice of the appointment of an arbitrator or of the arbitral proceedings or was otherwise unable to present his case; (iv) the award deals with a dispute not contemplated by or not falling within the terms of the submission, or contains decisions on matters beyond the scope (the offending part can be severed if separable); (v) the composition of the tribunal or the procedure was not in accordance with the agreement. Grounds under s.34(2)(b) - found by the court: the subject-matter is not capable of settlement by arbitration under the law for the time being in force; or the award is in conflict with the public policy of India. Explanation 1 (2015): an award is in conflict with public policy only if (i) its making was induced or affected by fraud or corruption or was in violation of s.75 (confidentiality of conciliation) or s.81; (ii) it is in contravention with the fundamental policy of Indian law; or (iii) it is in conflict with the most basic notions of morality or justice; Explanation 2: the test as to whether there is contravention of the fundamental policy of Indian law shall not entail a review on the merits of the dispute. s.34(2A) (2015): in a domestic arbitration (not an international commercial arbitration), an award may also be set aside if the court finds that it is vitiated by patent illegality appearing on the face of the award; but an award shall not be set aside merely on the ground of an erroneous application of the law or by reappreciation of evidence.

Procedure and limitation: s.34(3) - the application must be made within three months from the date on which the party making it received the award (or the disposal of a request under s.33); the court may entertain it within a further period of 30 days if sufficiently satisfied that the applicant was prevented by sufficient cause, but not thereafter (Union of India v. Popular Construction Co., 2001 - s.5 Limitation Act does not apply; Simplex Infrastructures Ltd. v. Union of India, 2019 - the 30 days are in addition and not extendable). s.34(4) - on request, the court may adjourn the proceedings for a period to allow the tribunal to resume proceedings or take such other action as will eliminate the grounds for setting aside; s.34(5)-(6) (2015) - the application must be accompanied by an affidavit of prior notice to the other party and shall be disposed of expeditiously within one year from the date of service of notice.

Public policy jurisprudence: Renusagar Power Co. v. General Electric Co. (1994) - narrow meaning of public policy for foreign awards (fundamental policy of Indian law, interests of India, justice or morality); ONGC Ltd. v. Saw Pipes Ltd. (2003) - widened public policy for domestic awards to include 'patent illegality'; ONGC Ltd. v. Western Geco International Ltd. (2014) - added the 'judicial approach', natural justice and 'Wednesbury' unreasonableness; Associate Builders v. Delhi Development Authority (2015) - contours of public policy: fundamental policy, interest of India, justice or morality, patent illegality; the court must not act as an appellate forum; the tribunal is the final judge of facts; Ssangyong Engineering & Construction Co. Ltd. v. NHAI (2019) - after the 2015 Amendment the Saw Pipes/Western Geco expansions are no longer good law; the grounds are only those in the Explanations to s.34(2)(b) and the patent illegality ground (domestic only); NHAI v. Progressive-MVR (2018); Delhi Airport Metro Express Pvt. Ltd. v. DMRC (2021 and 2022) - patent illegality and the curative petition (the court set aside an award on a patent-illegality basis and later criticised its own approach to interference in the curative petition judgment); Patel Engineering Ltd. v. North Eastern Electric Power Corp. (2020) - the limits of interference with awards.

Court's power to modify awards - Gayatri Balasamy v. ISG Novasoft Technologies Ltd. (30 April 2025, Constitution Bench, 4:1): courts exercising jurisdiction under ss.34 and 37 have a limited power to modify an arbitral award: (a) to sever the invalid portion from the valid portion if they are separable (partial setting aside); (b) to correct clerical, computational or typographical errors apparent on the face of the record; (c) in appropriate circumstances to modify post-award interest; and the Supreme Court may, in exercise of its Art 142 powers, modify an award in rare cases with great care and caution, consistent with the Act's limited scope; courts cannot rewrite the award on its merits or reappreciate evidence; Justice K.V. Viswanathan dissented (courts can only set aside). Remand (s.34(4)) remains a separate tool.

Finality and enforcement (ss.35-36): the award is final and binding on the parties and persons claiming under them (s.35); it is enforced under the CPC in the same manner as if it were a decree of the court (s.36(1)) once the time for making an application under s.34 has expired, or such application has been refused. s.36(2) (2015) - the mere filing of a s.34 application does not by itself render the award unenforceable unless the court grants a stay on a separate application; s.36(3) - the court may grant a stay subject to such conditions as it deems fit, and for a money decree shall have due regard to the provisions for grant of stay of a money decree under the CPC (Order XLI Rule 5); proviso (2021) - where the court is satisfied that a prima facie case is made out that the arbitration agreement or contract which is the basis of the award, or the making of the award, was induced or affected by fraud or corruption, it shall stay the award unconditionally pending disposal of the s.34 application (this proviso applies to all court cases arising out of arbitral proceedings irrespective of when commenced). Bank guarantees, security and deposit conditions on stay follow. Enforcement of domestic awards is before the court as defined in s.2(1)(e) at the place where the assets are (or seat); Sundaram Finance Ltd. v. NEPC India Ltd. (1999) - Part I applies to enforcement proceedings even before the 1996 Act formally; s.42 limited.

Appeals (s.37): an appeal lies from (1)(a) an order refusing to refer the parties to arbitration under s.8; (b) an order granting or refusing to grant any measure under s.9; (c) an order setting aside or refusing to set aside an arbitral award under s.34; and (2) from an order of the arbitral tribunal (a) accepting the plea referred to in s.16(2) or (3) (no jurisdiction / excess of authority); (b) granting or refusing interim measure under s.17; to the court authorised by law to hear appeals from original decrees of the court passing the order (s.37(1)); no second appeal, but nothing takes away the right to appeal to the Supreme Court (s.37(3)) - i.e., SLP under Art 136. Section 37 jurisdiction is narrower than appellate jurisdiction over decrees and the appellate court does not re-examine the merits (MMTC Ltd. v. Vedanta Ltd., 2019; Konkan Railway Corp. v. Chenab Bridge Project, 2023). orders under s.11 are not appealable under s.37 (only SLP under Art 136).

International commercial arbitration and domestic awards: an award in an ICA held in India is a 'domestic award' (s.2(7)) and is enforceable under s.36; patent illegality not available in an ICA (s.34(2A) proviso). Enforcement of awards made in India but against foreign parties, and enforcement of foreign awards in India under Part II. Institutional arbitration: ICA (Indian Council of Arbitration, 1965); ICADR (1995) - since taken over by NDIAC; New Delhi International Arbitration Centre Act 2019 (NDIAC) - institution of national importance; MCIA (Mumbai Centre for International Arbitration, 2016); Delhi International Arbitration Centre (DIAC; Delhi High Court); International Arbitration and Mediation Centre (IAMC), Hyderabad (2021); Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC; 2025 Rules); International Chamber of Commerce (ICC); London Court of International Arbitration (LCIA); UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules. The Arbitration Council of India (Part IA) has not been constituted [VERIFY].

Foreign awards - Part II, Chapter I (New York Convention, 1958; India acceded 1960; reciprocity reservation and commercial reservation): s.44 - 'foreign award' - an arbitral award on differences between persons arising out of legal relationships, contractual or not, considered commercial under Indian law, made on or after 11 October 1960 in pursuance of an agreement in writing to which the New York Convention applies and in one of such territories as the Central Government, by notification in the Official Gazette, declares to be territories to which the Convention applies. s.45 - power of a judicial authority to refer the parties to arbitration (at the request of a party, unless it finds that the agreement is null and void, inoperative or incapable of being performed). s.46 - foreign awards are binding on the persons as between whom they were made. s.47 - evidence: the party applying for enforcement shall produce the original award or a duly authenticated copy, the original agreement or certified copy, and evidence to prove that it is a foreign award (translation if not in English). s.48 - conditions for enforcement: enforcement may be refused at the request of the party against whom it is invoked only if that party furnishes proof that (a) the parties were under some incapacity or the agreement is not valid; (b) he was not given proper notice or was unable to present his case; (c) the award deals with a difference not contemplated by or beyond the submission (severable); (d) the composition of the tribunal or procedure was not in accordance with the agreement or the law of the country where the arbitration took place; (e) the award has not yet become binding or has been set aside or suspended by a competent authority of the country in which, or under the law of which, it was made; or the court finds that (a) the subject-matter is not capable of settlement by arbitration under Indian law, or (b) enforcement would be contrary to the public policy of India (Explanation 1: fraud or corruption; violation of s.75/s.81; contravention of the fundamental policy of Indian law; conflict with the most basic notions of morality or justice; Explanation 2: no review on merits). s.49 - once the court is satisfied that the award is enforceable it is deemed to be a decree of that court. s.50 - appeal: lies from an order refusing to refer under s.45 and refusing to enforce under s.48 (not from an order enforcing); no second appeal but Art 136 (the 2015 Amendment reiterated). s.51-52 - saving; Chapter II - Geneva Convention awards (ss.53-60).

Foreign awards jurisprudence: Renusagar (1994); Shri Lal Mahal Ltd. v. Progetto Grano S.p.A. (2014) - public policy under s.48 is narrower than under s.34; the court does not review merits; Shin-Etsu Chemical Co. Ltd. v. Aksh Optifibre Ltd. (2005) - the court at the s.45 stage applies a prima facie test (later modified by the 2015 amendment); Vijay Karia v. Prysmian Cavi E Sistemi SRL (2020) - the grounds under s.48 are exhaustive; the enforcing court shall not go into the merits; the expression 'public policy' is to be given a narrow meaning; the discretion to refuse enforcement is limited; Government of India v. Vedanta Ltd. (2020) - the seat of arbitration is not necessarily the place where the hearing is held; the law governing the arbitration agreement; Bhatia International (2002) overruled prospectively by BALCO; Union of India v. Reliance Industries (2018). Enforcement: foreign award enforceable as a decree once found enforceable; limitation for enforcement is governed by the Limitation Act (Art 136 - 12 years).

Practical road-map for enforcement: domestic award - wait for s.34 period; apply for enforcement under s.36 in the proper court (Order XXI CPC applies); foreign award - file application under s.47-49 in the High Court (original side) having jurisdiction over the assets; no further proceedings to challenge (s.34 is unavailable to foreign awards, but s.48 objections can be raised); appeals per s.50.

Latest developments in arbitration law (2023-2026): Cox and Kings (Dec 2023); Interplay (Dec 2023); CORE (Nov 2024) on unilateral appointment; Gayatri Balasamy (Apr 2025) on modification; Mediation Council of India (Aug 2026); the Expert Committee on Arbitration (Feb 2024) and the Draft Arbitration and Conciliation (Amendment) Bill 2024 - proposals include statutory recognition of emergency arbitrators, an appellate arbitral tribunal, a clearer definition of seat/venue, limiting court intervention, and mandatory institutional timelines; the Supreme Court and the Chief Justice in 2026 have urged making India a hub for institutional arbitration and have criticised delay at the enforcement stage (e.g., enforcement petitions pending for years) [VERIFY].

sections.title: PIL: Meaning, Evolution, Constitutional Basis, Types and Judicial Techniques
sections.overview: Where PIL came from, why courts allowed strangers to sue, and the innovative remedies (epistolary jurisdiction, commissions, continuing mandamus) that define Indian public law.
must_know: Meaning: litigation for the protection of the public interest or the general interest of a community, as distinct from a private dispute; initiated by a public-spirited person or by the court itself on behalf of persons who cannot approach the court because of poverty, ignorance, disability or social disadvantage. It is not defined in any statute; it is a judicial innovation under Art 32 (Supreme Court) and Art 226 (High Courts). Also called 'social action litigation' (Upendra Baxi) and 'epistolary jurisdiction' when begun by a letter.

Evolution: until the late 1970s Indian courts followed the traditional rule that only a 'person aggrieved' (one whose own legal right had been infringed) could invoke the court. After the Emergency (1975-77), judges such as Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer and Justice P.N. Bhagwati (and later Justice Kuldip Singh, Justice J.S. Verma and Justice Chinnappa Reddy) relaxed the rule of locus standi to make justice accessible to the poor. Early signals: Mumbai Kamgar Sabha v. Abdulbhai (1976); Municipal Council, Ratlam v. Vardhichand (1980) (a community of residents compelled the municipality to provide drains; s.133 CrPC); the first reported PIL: Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar (1979) - brought on the basis of a newspaper report by advocate Kapila Hingorani about undertrial prisoners in Bihar jails, leading to recognition of the right to speedy trial and free legal aid under Art 21.

Constitutional basis: Art 32 (enforcement of Fundamental Rights; the Supreme Court can issue 'directions, orders or writs'), Art 226 (High Courts, for enforcement of Fundamental Rights and 'for any other purpose'), Art 142 (complete justice), Art 21 (expanded to include dignity, livelihood, health, environment), Art 39A (legal aid), Art 51A(g) (environment). Art 12 'State' is widely read so that PIL can reach authorities and sometimes private bodies performing public functions. Court uses Art 14 to scrutinise arbitrary State action. DPSPs (Arts 38, 39, 41, 42, 43, 47, 48A) are read into Art 21.

Locus standi - traditional v. liberalised: traditional - the petitioner must show the infringement of his own legal right; liberalised - 'any member of the public having sufficient interest' can maintain an action for judicial redress for public injury arising from breach of a public duty or violation of a constitutional or legal provision, provided he acts bona fide and not for personal gain or private profit or political motive (S.P. Gupta v. Union of India, 1981, the Judges' Transfer case - Justice Bhagwati). Representative standing: for the poor and disabled (Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India, 1984; Peoples' Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India, 1982); citizen standing: for matters of public concern (e.g., environment; public property); organisational standing: NGOs, bar associations and trade unions (Fertilizer Corporation Kamgar Union v. Union of India, 1981 - a union may challenge sale of plant; Akhil Bharatiya Soshit Karamchari Sangh v. Union of India, 1981).

Types of PIL: (1) representative PIL on behalf of the disadvantaged; (2) citizen/public-spirited PIL (environment, corruption, governance); (3) epistolary jurisdiction - letters or postcards treated as writ petitions (Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration, 1978/1980; Bandhua Mukti Morcha, 1984); (4) suo motu cognizance - on the basis of newspaper reports, letters or events (e.g., the Aravalli Hills and stray dogs matters, 2025-26); (5) PIL against the State, public authorities, and even private persons where public duty is involved; (6) interest-group PILs (consumer, labour, women, children); (7) amicus curiae-assisted PILs. PIL in the Supreme Court is dealt with by the PIL Cell (letters to the Chief Justice) and the Registry's circulars.

Judicial techniques developed in PIL: (a) relaxation of procedure (letter as petition; no formal pleadings; no costs); (b) appointment of commissions of inquiry/ socio-legal commissions to collect facts (Bandhua Mukti Morcha; Sheela Barse); (c) amicus curiae (e.g., M.C. Mehta cases; Parmanand Katara); (d) expert and monitoring committees (Central Empowered Committee - forests; Monitoring Committee - Delhi sealing; EPCA - Delhi air); (e) continuing mandamus - the court retains jurisdiction and issues periodic directions (Vineet Narain v. Union of India, 1998; Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan, 1997; T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India, 1996-; M.C. Mehta); (f) interim directions and 'public law compensation' (Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar, 1983; Nilabati Behera, 1993; M.C. Mehta v. Union of India - Oleum Gas, 1987); (g) filling legislative vacuum with guidelines under Art 141 until Parliament acts (Vishaka; Lakshmi v. Union of India (acid sale); Prakash Singh v. Union of India (police reforms, 2006)); (h) reading international conventions into Art 21 (Vishaka); (i) cost orders and exemplary costs on frivolous PIL; (j) liberal interpretation of 'State' (Ajay Hasia, 1981).

Arguments for and against: PIL promotes access to justice, accountability, rule of law and protection of the vulnerable; critics point to judicial overreach, separation of powers, lack of expertise (the Supreme Court itself in 2026 said 'We are not scientists' while rejecting a PIL on urban growth around airports), docket burden, and misuse for publicity, private or political motives. Courts have laid down self-restraint principles (see 9.P4).

Role of Bar and legal aid: advocates and law students may file PIL as petitioners-in-person; legal aid authorities assist; Advocates may be appointed as amici; PIL petitions need a verified petition and, in many High Courts, an affidavit disclosing credentials (Balwant Singh Chaufal, 2010).

sections.title: PIL Procedure: Who Can File, Where, Supreme Court Guidelines (1988) on Letter-Petitions, Categories Entertained and Excluded, Costs and Interim Relief
sections.articles: Arts 32, 226; Supreme Court Rules 2013; Supreme Court Handbook on PIL; High Court PIL Rules
sections.overview: The mechanics of filing a PIL and the categories the Supreme Court listed for letter-petitions: both the included and the excluded categories are frequently asked.
must_know: Filing: a PIL may be filed by any person or organisation (including a petitioner-in-person) before the Supreme Court under Art 32 or before a High Court under Art 226; a letter or postcard addressed to the Chief Justice or a judge may be treated as a writ petition (epistolary). The petitioner discloses his identity, credentials and the public interest involved, and (under many High Court PIL Rules) files an affidavit stating that he has no personal interest and has made adequate inquiry; the court may require the petitioner to deposit costs or security. The petition names the State/authority and 'proper parties'; notice is issued; the court may seek reports from commissions or committees; relief may be interim.

Supreme Court's guidelines for PIL (1988, as revised): the Court will ordinarily entertain letter-petitions/PIL in respect of: (1) bonded labour matters; (2) neglected children; (3) non-payment of minimum wages to workers and exploitation of casual workers, and complaints of violation of labour laws (except in individual cases); (4) petitions from jails complaining of harassment, for premature release, release after 14 years, death in jail, transfer, release on personal bond, and personal liberty issues of prisoners; (5) petitions seeking speedy trial as a fundamental right; (6) petitions complaining of police inaction in regard to criminal offences; (7) petitions against police for refusing to register a case, harassment by police and death in police custody; (8) petitions against atrocities on women, in particular harassment of bride, bride burning, rape, murder, kidnapping; (9) petitions complaining of harassment or torture of villagers by co-villagers or police from persons belonging to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes and economically backward classes; (10) petitions pertaining to environmental pollution, disturbance of ecological balance, drugs, food adulteration, maintenance of heritage and culture, antiques, forests and wildlife and other matters of public importance; (11) petitions from riot-victims; (12) family pension. [VERIFY exact list in the Supreme Court Handbook.]

Categories NOT ordinarily entertained as PIL (letter-petitions): (1) landlord-tenant matters; (2) service matters and those pertaining to pension and gratuity; (3) complaints against Central/State Government departments and local bodies, except those relating to matters listed above; (4) admission to medical and engineering colleges; (5) petitions for early hearing of matters pending in High Courts and subordinate courts. Dr. Duryodhan Sahu v. Jitendra Kumar Mishra (1998): PIL cannot be entertained in service matters, especially by strangers; the remedy is before the Administrative Tribunal; Rajiv Ranjan Singh 'Lalan' v. Union of India (2006) reaffirmed that service matters are excluded; Ashok Kumar Pandey v. State of West Bengal (2004).

Judicial reluctance in specific areas: criminal prosecutions - a stranger cannot normally intervene (Janata Dal v. H.S. Chowdhary, 1992; Simranjit Singh Mann v. Union of India, 1992 - mercy petitions); tax and contract disputes; policy matters (court will not substitute its opinion; e.g., Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India, 2000 - Sardar Sarovar dam); tender and commercial decisions (Raunaq International Ltd. v. I.V.R. Construction Ltd., 1999; Jagdish Mandal v. State of Orissa, 2007 - judicial review is of decision-making process; Tata Cellular v. Union of India, 1994); religious and cultural matters - locus standi examined stricter (2026 observations in the Sabarimala reference); scientific and technical issues - experts to be consulted (We are not scientists, 2026).

Costs: the court may dismiss a frivolous or vexatious PIL with exemplary costs; costs may be imposed on the petitioner or the advocate; courts have jailed or fined petitioners for false PIL (e.g., Holicow Pictures Pvt. Ltd. v. Prem Chandra Mishra, 2007 - costs for PIL used as a blackmailing device; Dattaraj Nathuji Thaware v. State of Maharashtra, 2005 - 'PIL is not a pill or a panacea for all wrongs'; Kushum Lata v. Union of India, 2006). In 2026 the Supreme Court dismissed 25 PILs filed by a single advocate-petitioner in one stroke (10 April 2026) telling him not to rush to court (Sachin Gupta v. Union of India, WP(C) 444/2026) [VERIFY].

Interim and final relief: interim injunctions; interim compensation; directions to the State to implement laws; appointing committees; monitoring; closing the case when the grievance is redressed; 'Public law compensation' under Arts 32/226 for violation of Art 21 is distinct from tort damages (Nilabati Behera, 1993).

PIL and other proceedings: PIL cannot be used for private disputes or to enforce contractual rights; a person who has a personal remedy (e.g., consumer forum, civil suit) is generally relegated; a pending PIL on the same issue ordinarily bars repetitive PILs; res judicata applies in PIL in a limited manner (Forward Construction Co. v. Prabhat Mandal, 1986 - constructive res judicata applies in public interest matters; also State of Karnataka v. All India Manufacturers Organisation, 2006 - Bangalore-Mysore Infrastructure; PIL of public-spirited persons not barred for want of specific injury).

Public interest litigation in High Courts: Art 226 jurisdiction; many High Courts (Allahabad, Delhi, Bombay, Calcutta, Madras, Gujarat, Patna, Orissa, Punjab and Haryana etc.) have PIL Rules; Division Bench hears PIL; reporting by amicus.

State of Maharashtra (1983) - women prisoners; Sheela Barse v. Union of India (1986) - children in jail; Veena Sethi v. State of Bihar (1982) - forgotten prisoners; Kadra Pahadiya v. Mehta v. Kamal Nath (1997) - public trust doctrine; T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India (1996-) - forests; Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) - precautionary principle and polluter pays are part of Indian law; Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India (1996) - polluter pays; Subhash Kumar v. The Supreme Court has also taken suo motu cognisance in matters like Aravalli definition (2025), stray dogs (2025), prison overcrowding, and sexual violence (Nirbhaya-type cases).
