sections.title: Limits, Abuse and Regulation of PIL: Balwant Singh Chaufal Guidelines, Judicial Overreach, Docket Restructuring and 2025-26 Developments
sections.overview: Courts have tightened PIL: guidelines for filtering petitions, costs for abuse and, in 2026, a push to restructure decades-old continuing mandamus cases. Learn the guidelines and the latest rulings.
must_know: State of Uttaranchal v. Balwant Singh Chaufal (2010, Supreme Court): comprehensive guidelines to check abuse of PIL: (1) the courts must encourage genuine and bona fide PIL and effectively discourage and curb the PIL filed for extraneous considerations; (2) each High Court should prepare its own Rules for encouraging genuine PIL and discouraging PIL filed with oblique motives; (3) the court should be prima facie satisfied regarding the correctness of the contents of the petition; (4) the court must be satisfied about the credentials of the petitioner; (5) the court should be satisfied that the petition involves a larger public interest, gravity and urgency of the matter; (6) the court should ensure that the petition does not involve personal gain, private motive or oblique motive; (7) the court should not entertain PIL that has publicity interest or political interest; (8) petitioners filing frivolous PIL should be burdened with exemplary costs; (9) the courts should take care of the public interest in matters such as service, family and contractual disputes. The Court also directed that certain matters (such as those under the 1988 guidelines) be examined carefully; Dr. B. Singh v. Union of India (2004) - 'PIL is a weapon which has to be used with great care and circumspection'; Ashok Kumar Pandey v. State of W.B. (2004) - judges must be careful to see that the public interest is not a cloak for private gain; Guruvayur Devaswom Managing Committee v. C.K. Rajan (2003) - guidelines on PIL (a PIL involving public interest and not mere busybody); Kushum Lata v. Union of India (2006) - costs; State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977) - 'busybodies'.

Doctrinal limits: (a) separation of powers - the court should not legislate or perform executive functions but can fill gaps in the law and enforce fundamental rights (Supreme Court Bar Association v. Union of India, 1998; Divisional Manager, Aravali Golf Club v. Chander Hass, 2008 - judges must not overstep; Asif Hameed v. State of J&K, 1989); (b) technical and scientific issues - rely on experts; (c) political questions - courts do not decide purely political questions; (d) policy matters - review limited; (e) alternative remedies; (f) personal-liberty PIL (habeas corpus) is relaxed; (g) criminal matters - strangers are not allowed to interfere with prosecution (Janata Dal v. H.S. Chowdhary, 1992), but a PIL to compel investigation of a serious crime is allowed in rare cases (Vineet Narain; Sakiri Vasu).

Abuse categories (the 'four P's' - 2026 remarks): in May 2026 a Constitution Bench (nine-judge Sabarimala reference) comprising CJI Surya Kant and Justices B.V. Nagarathna, M.M. Sundresh, Ahsanuddin Amanullah, Aravind Kumar, Augustine George Masih, Prasanna B. Varale, R. Mahadevan and Joymalya Bagchi remarked that PIL has become 'Private, Publicity, Paisa and Political Interest Litigation' and that only real and genuine PILs would be entertained; the Court also questioned how a newspaper article gives a cause of action [reported 5 May 2026; VERIFY]. In April 2026 the Court in the same reference emphasised stricter locus standi norms in faith cases, noting that the 2006 Sabarimala PIL by a stranger would have been dismissed under today's standard [VERIFY]. On 10 April 2026 the CJI Surya Kant Bench dismissed 25 PILs filed by the same advocate in one go (Sachin Gupta v. Union of India, WP(C) 444/2026).

Docket restructuring of continuing-mandamus PILs: on 13 April 2026 the Bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justice Bagchi restructured the forest conservation litigation In re: T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad (instituted 1995); in March 2026 (M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, WP(C) 13381/1984, decided 11 March 2026) and in the Taj Trapezium case (2026 INSC 381) the Court closed decades-old M.C. Mehta petitions and split the pending issues into fresh suo motu proceedings and High Court proceedings under Art 226; the Court said it was rationalising its docket and regulating the use of continuing mandamus [VERIFY citations].

Environmental and animal-welfare PIL (2025-26): Aravalli Hills - the Supreme Court in November 2025 accepted a Ministry committee's definition (a landform of 100 metres or more local relief) in the matter; after criticism it took suo motu cognisance (In re: Definition of Aravalli Hills and Ranges and Ancillary Issues), stayed its own ruling on 29 December 2025 and constituted an independent expert committee; in 2026 it said it would not allow anybody to touch the Aravalli range for now and that the new committee must have broader public participation (25 May 2026); stray dogs - suo motu 'In re: City Hounded by Strays, Kids Pay the Price' (July-August 2025 orders; final judgment on 19 May 2026 held that the Animal Birth Control Rules 2023 confer no unqualified right on stray dogs to inhabit particular premises while the State must manage stray dogs scientifically through sterilisation, vaccination and sheltering) [VERIFY]; the Court also said 'We are not scientists' in declining a PIL on urban growth around airports after the Air India AI171 crash [VERIFY].
Role of the High Court and amicus: High Courts increasingly use committees; some have special PIL benches; amici ensure assistance; costs for frivolous cases; and notice to the Advocate-General.

Reform proposals: statutory regulation; Law Commission 177th/ 192nd reports; specialised PIL benches; mandatory pre-filing disclosure of previous petitions; deposits; limit on 'professional petitioners'; use of legal aid authorities to vet PIL; digital filing with credentials verification.

sections.title: Advocates Act, 1961: Bar Councils, Enrolment, Right to Practise, Senior Advocates, Right of Audience
sections.articles: Advocates Act 1961 ss.3-34, 45-49; Supreme Court Rules 2013 (AoR); Bar Council of India Rules Parts I-IV
sections.overview: The statutory machinery that regulates the legal profession. The Act has a regular set of testable sections.
must_know: The Advocates Act 1961 (on the recommendation of the Law Commission's 14th Report and the All India Bar Committee) amends and consolidates the law relating to legal practitioners and provides for the constitution of Bar Councils and an All-India Bar; it abolished the old classes of legal practitioners (pleaders, vakils, attorneys) and created a single class - 'advocates' (s.29). Chapters: II Bar Councils (ss.3-15); III Admission and enrolment of advocates (ss.16-28); IV Right to practise (ss.29-34); V Conduct of advocates (ss.35-44); VI Miscellaneous (ss.45-60). In force from 19 May 1961 (the Act was brought into force progressively).

State Bar Councils (s.3): a Bar Council for each State (and for Delhi and the Union Territories); composition: the Advocate-General of the State as ex officio member and 15 members (where the electorate is up to 5,000), 20 members (5,001-10,000) or 25 members (above 10,000) elected by advocates on the State roll from amongst themselves (proportional representation by single transferable vote); term of five years (s.8); Chairman and Vice-Chairman elected by the Council [VERIFY section]. Functions (s.6): admit persons as advocates on its roll; prepare and maintain such roll; entertain and determine cases of misconduct against advocates on its roll; safeguard the rights, privileges and interests of advocates; promote and support law reform; manage and invest its funds; provide for the election of its members; organise legal aid to the poor in the prescribed manner; promote legal education and lay down standards in consultation with the BCI and universities.

Bar Council of India (s.4): consists of the Attorney-General of India and the Solicitor-General of India (ex officio) and one member elected by each State Bar Council from among its members; Chairman and Vice-Chairman elected by the Council; term of five years [VERIFY the extension of terms in recent years]. Functions (s.7): lay down standards of professional conduct and etiquette for advocates; lay down procedure to be followed by its disciplinary committee and those of each State Bar Council; safeguard rights, privileges and interests of advocates; promote and support law reform; deal with and dispose of any matter arising under the Act referred to it by a State Bar Council; exercise general supervision and control over State Bar Councils; promote legal education and lay down standards in consultation with the universities and State Bar Councils; recognise universities whose degree in law shall be a qualification for enrolment (and visit and inspect them); conduct seminars; organise legal aid; recognise foreign qualifications in law on a reciprocal basis; manage and invest funds; provide for the election of its members. s.49 - the BCI's general power to make rules, including on standards of professional conduct and etiquette (s.49(1)(c)), on dress to be worn by advocates (s.49(1)(gg)), conditions subject to which an advocate may practise, and the disciplinary procedure. Committees: the Disciplinary Committee (three persons: two elected from members and one co-opted advocate; the senior-most is the Chairman), the Executive Committee, the Legal Aid Committee and others (ss.9-10B).

Senior and other advocates (s.16): two classes - senior advocates and other advocates; an advocate may with his consent be designated as a senior advocate if the Supreme Court or a High Court is of the opinion that by virtue of his ability, standing at the Bar or special knowledge or experience in law he is deserving of such distinction; senior advocates are subject to restrictions specified by the BCI in the interests of the profession. Indira Jaising v. Supreme Court of India (2017): guidelines for designation - a Permanent Committee (Chief Justice, two senior-most judges, Attorney-General and a member of the Bar nominated), a point-based system (100 points - years of practice, reported judgments, publications, personality test), consideration by the Full Court; in 2023 (Indira Jaising v. Supreme Court of India, Jan 2023) the Court reviewed the point system and clarified its application, relying on a holistic assessment [VERIFY]. A senior advocate cannot file vakalatnama or accept instructions directly from a client; must appear with an Advocate-on-Record in the Supreme Court; cannot draft pleadings (BCI Rules, Part VI Chapter I). Advocates-on-Record (Supreme Court Rules 2013, Order IV): only an AoR (who has passed the AoR examination and trained for one year under an AoR) can file matters in the Supreme Court.

Admission and enrolment: s.17 - State Bar Council prepares and maintains a roll (State roll) of advocates; s.18 - transfer of name from one State roll to another; s.22 - certificate of enrolment; s.24 - qualifications: (a) a citizen of India (nationals of other countries admitted on reciprocal basis); (b) has completed 21 years of age; (c) has obtained a degree in law from a recognised university (three-year course after a graduate degree, or a five-year integrated course) or a foreign qualification recognised by the BCI; (d) fulfils such other conditions as the State Bar Council may specify; (e) has paid the enrolment fee (not exceeding Rs 600 to the State Bar Council and Rs 150 to the BCI; Rs 125 and Rs 25 for SC/ST - total Rs 750 general / Rs 125 per [VERIFY]) - Gaurav Kumar v. Union of India (30 July 2024): State Bar Councils cannot charge enrolment fee beyond the statutory fee. s.24A - disqualifications for enrolment: (a) conviction for an offence involving moral turpitude; (b) conviction for an offence under the Untouchability (Offences) Act 1955 (now Protection of Civil Rights Act); (c) dismissal or removal from employment or office under the State on a charge involving moral turpitude; disqualification (a) and (b) ceases after two years from release [VERIFY]. s.26 - disposal of applications; s.26A - removal of names from the roll (on death, or on the request of the advocate, or for any other reason); s.30 - right to practise (see below). BCI Verification Rules 2015: Certificate of Practice and Place of Practice; All India Bar Examination (AIBE) - mandatory for enrolled advocates to obtain a Certificate of Practice (BCI Rules, Part VI; AIBE upheld in Bar Council of India v. Bonnie Foi Law College, 2023: the BCI has the power to conduct the AIBE after enrolment, as a post-enrolment test for competence and a pre-condition to the certificate; the Court reiterated that the exam does not violate Art 19(1)(g)).

Right to practise (Chapter IV): s.29 - only advocates are recognised as a class of persons entitled to practise law; s.30 - every advocate whose name is entered in the State roll is entitled as of right to practise throughout the territories to which the Act extends in (i) all courts including the Supreme Court; (ii) before any tribunal or person legally authorised to take evidence; (iii) before any other authority or person before whom such advocate is by or under any law for the time being in force entitled to practise (s.30 came into force on 15 June 2011); s.32 - power of the court to permit appearances by non-advocates in a particular case; s.33 - advocates alone are entitled to practise (no person unless enrolled as an advocate can practise in any court or before any authority, subject to the Act or other law); s.34 - High Court's power to make rules laying down conditions subject to which an advocate shall be permitted to practise in the High Court and the courts subordinate to it; s.35 - misconduct (see 9.E2). Pre-audience (s.23): (1) the Attorney-General of India has pre-audience over all other advocates; (2) the Solicitor-General; (3) Additional Solicitors-General; (4) the Advocates-General of States (in their respective States; in the order of seniority of the States for outside courts); (5) senior advocates; (6) other advocates (inter se seniority according to date of enrolment). A senior advocate gets precedence over other advocates.

Persons illegally practising (s.45): any person who practises in any court or before any other authority or person, in contravention of s.33, is punishable with imprisonment up to six months. Advocates Welfare Fund Act 2001; Bar Council of India Rules on legal education (Rules of Legal Education 2008; 3-year and 5-year courses; Standards).

Foreign lawyers: Bar Council of India v. A.K. Balaji (13 March 2018): foreign law firms and foreign lawyers cannot practise litigation or non-litigation in India (the practice of law includes non-litigious work) but may visit on a 'fly-in fly-out' basis for a temporary period to advise on foreign law and international arbitration; the BCI Rules for Registration and Regulation of Foreign Lawyers and Foreign Law Firms in India 2022 (as amended in 2025) permit registration of foreign lawyers and firms to practise foreign law and international legal matters on a reciprocal basis, excluding litigation and matters requiring Indian enrolment [VERIFY 2025 amendments].

Legal education and bar: Law Commission 266th Report (2017) on the Advocates Act (suggestions on regulation of legal profession, strikes, and disciplinary system); Advocates (Amendment) Bill 2025 (draft, circulated February 2025; withdrawn after protests) [VERIFY].

sections.title: Professional and Other Misconduct (s.35), Disciplinary Committees, Procedure, Punishments, Appeals and Leading Misconduct Cases
sections.articles: Advocates Act ss.35-44, 49; BCI Rules Part VII (Disciplinary Committee procedure)
sections.overview: Chapter V of the Act. Know the procedure, who decides, what penalties exist, and the cases on what counts as misconduct.
must_know: s.35 - Punishment of advocates for professional or other misconduct: where, on receipt of a complaint or otherwise, a State Bar Council has reason to believe that any advocate on its roll has been guilty of professional or other misconduct, it shall refer the case for disposal to its Disciplinary Committee; the Disciplinary Committee after giving the advocate concerned and the Advocate-General of the State an opportunity of being heard may (a) dismiss the complaint or, where the proceedings were initiated at the instance of the State Bar Council, direct that the proceedings be filed; (b) reprimand the advocate; (c) suspend the advocate from practice for such period as it may deem fit; (d) remove the name of the advocate from the State roll of advocates. s.35(4): where an advocate is suspended from practice, he is debarred during the period of suspension from practising in any court or before any authority or person in India. The Bar Council of India's Disciplinary Committee has parallel powers in cases referred to it, and original powers over advocates of different States (s.36).

Meaning of 'misconduct': the Act does not define it. It covers professional misconduct and 'other' misconduct (conduct unbecoming even outside professional work). Bar Council of Maharashtra v. M.V. Dabholkar (1975): misconduct includes conduct that disgraces the profession; the Bar Council is the proper body to judge; Noratanmal Chouraria v. M.R. Murli (2004): the court should presume only if misconduct is established; V.C. Rangadurai v. D. Gopalan (1979): professional misconduct arises when an advocate breaches his duty to a client; the advocate-client relationship is fiduciary; the Supreme Court upheld the Bar Council's punishment although the complainant was not the client; In re: Vinay Chandra Mishra (1995): a senior advocate was held guilty of contempt of the Supreme Court and suspended from practice for three years - the Court held it may suspend an advocate's right to practise as part of contempt jurisdiction (Art 129) and that an advocate is an officer of the court and must maintain its dignity; Pravin C. Shah v. K.A. Mohd. Ali (2001): the High Court cannot, in contempt proceedings, deprive an advocate of his right to practise (this lies exclusively with the Bar Council under s.35); the court may refer the matter to the Bar Council; Bar Council of India v. High Court of Kerala (2004): the High Court can prevent an advocate from appearing in a court by an order but has no power to debar from practice; R.D. Saxena v. Balram Prasad Sharma (2000): an advocate has no lien over papers/documents of a client for unpaid fees and cannot withhold them - failure to return is professional misconduct; the Court also held that an advocate who refuses to return documents is guilty and was suspended for six months.

Illustrative misconduct under s.35 and BCI Rules: (1) negligence or non-appearance after accepting a brief (Chandra Shekhar Soni v. Bar Council of Rajasthan, 1983; Harish Chandra Tiwari v. Baiju, 2002 - gross negligence); (2) misappropriation or non-accounting of client's money (P.D. Gupta v. Ram Murti, 1997); (3) acting against a former client; (4) fraudulent or dishonest conduct or forging documents; (5) bribery, influencing a judge or presiding officer or communicating privately with the judge (BCI Rules); (6) misbehaviour with court or judge (M.B. Sanghi v. High Court of Punjab and Haryana, 1991 - advocate abusing a judge; O.P. Sharma v. High Court of Punjab and Haryana, 2011); (7) striking and abstaining from courts (Ex-Capt. Harish Uppal v. Union of India, 2002; Krishnakant Tamrakar v. State of M.P., 2018); (8) soliciting work, touting and advertising (BCI Rule 36; Re: Rule 36); (9) charging a contingent fee/champerty; (10) appearing for a party whom the advocate previously advised for the opposite party; (11) engaging in business or employment in violation of BCI Rules; (12) fabrication of evidence; (13) improper conduct in the media (R.K. Anand v. Registrar, Delhi High Court, 2009 - senior advocate suspended for four months for attempting to subvert justice in the BMW hit-and-run case (sting operation); disqualified from being designated senior advocate for some time; the Court held that professional misconduct and contempt are different); (14) assault or insulting the judge/ witness; (15) conviction for moral turpitude offence; (16) conflict of interest; (17) conduct as a Law Officer in violation of rules (Sushma Suri v. Government of NCT of Delhi, 1999 - whether a salaried legal adviser is an advocate).

Standard of proof and procedure: disciplinary proceedings are quasi-judicial/ quasi-criminal; the Disciplinary Committee has the powers of a civil court for summoning, discovery and production of documents, receiving evidence on affidavits, issuing commissions (s.42); proceedings are judicial proceedings for the purposes of ss.193, 219 and 228 IPC (ss.229, 258 and 267 BNS) (s.42(2)); the complainant is not a party but his interest is considered; s.43 - costs of proceedings; s.44 - review of orders by the Disciplinary Committee (within 60 days). Procedure per Bar Council of India Rules Part VII: complaint with affidavit; reply; evidence; hearing; reasoned order; State Bar Council cannot hold proceedings in secret. Complaint may be made by a client, any person, a court (reference), or the Council itself suo motu; the Advocate-General is entitled to notice. The Disciplinary Committee should dispose of complaints within one year (s.36B).

s.36B (disposal of disciplinary proceedings): the Disciplinary Committee of a State Bar Council must dispose of a complaint within one year from the date of receipt of the complaint or initiation of proceedings suo motu; failing which the proceedings stand transferred to the BCI which shall dispose of them as if originally instituted; s.36A - changes in constitution of Disciplinary Committees; s.37 - appeal to the Bar Council of India: any person aggrieved by an order of the Disciplinary Committee of a State Bar Council made under s.35 (or the Advocate-General) may within 60 days of the date of communication of the order prefer an appeal to the BCI; the appeal is heard by a Disciplinary Committee of the BCI which may dismiss, modify, or set aside, with power to enhance the punishment; s.38 - appeal to the Supreme Court: any person aggrieved by an order of the Disciplinary Committee of the BCI made under s.35 or s.37 (or the Attorney-General or Advocate-General) may within 60 days prefer an appeal to the Supreme Court; the Supreme Court may pass such order as it deems fit; s.40 - stay of order; s.41 - alteration in the roll of advocates (when a name is removed etc.).

Reinstatement: an advocate removed from the roll may apply for restoration; the Disciplinary Committee may, after considering conduct, allow; s.26A (removal of names from roll) gives power to remove names of persons deceased or who have requested; the State Bar Council may restore.

Remedies for clients: complaint to the Bar Council; claim of negligence before the civil court (Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab (2005) on professional negligence principle; consumer forum - services rendered by advocates are not 'service' under the Consumer Protection Act (Bar of Indian Lawyers v. D.K. Gandhi (2024): the Supreme Court held in May 2024 that advocates/legal profession are not within the ambit of 'service' under the Consumer Protection Act 1986/2019); the earlier NCDRC decision in D.K. Gandhi PS Rao v. Bar of Indian Lawyers (2007) stayed [VERIFY details].

sections.title: Bar Council of India Rules (Part VI, Chapter II): Duty to Court, Client, Opponent and Colleagues; Fees and Accounts; Advertising; Other Employment; Senior Advocates; Dress
sections.articles: BCI Rules Part VI Chapters I-IV (framed under Advocates Act s.49(1)(c))
sections.overview: The core of the ethics paper. Learn each duty and a handful of rule numbers. (Rule numbers vary in published compilations; the substance is what is tested.)
must_know: Source and nature: the BCI Rules, Part VI, 'Rules Governing Advocates', framed under s.49(1)(c) of the Advocates Act, 'Standards of Professional Conduct and Etiquette'; Chapter I - Rules regarding senior advocates; Chapter II - Standards of Professional Conduct and Etiquette (Sections I-VII); Chapter III - Section on conditions for practising; Chapter IV - Dress; Rules are binding and breach can amount to professional misconduct under s.35.

Duty to the Court (Section I; Rules 1-10 [VERIFY numbers]): an advocate shall, during the presentation of his case and while acting before a court, conduct himself with dignity and self-respect, and shall use his best efforts to restrain and prevent his client from resorting to sharp or unfair practices (Rule 1); shall maintain a respectful attitude towards the courts, bearing in mind that the dignity of the judicial office is essential for a free community (Rule 2); shall not influence the decision of a court by any illegal or improper means; private communications with a judge relating to a pending case are forbidden (Rule 3); shall use his best efforts to restrain and prevent his client from resorting to unfair practices, and refuse to represent a client who persists (Rule 4); shall appear in court in the prescribed dress and presentable (Rule 5); shall not enter appearance, act, plead or practise before a court, tribunal or authority if the sole or any member thereof is related to the advocate as father, grandfather, son, grandson, uncle, brother, nephew, first cousin, husband, wife, mother, daughter, grandmother, aunt, sister, niece, father-in-law, etc. (Rule 6 - appearing before a relative); shall not wear bands or gowns in public places other than in courts except on ceremonial occasions (Rule 7); shall not appear for or against an organisation or institution, society or corporation if he is a member of the Executive Committee (Rule 8); shall not act or plead in any matter in which he is himself pecuniarily interested (Rule 9); shall not stand surety or certify the soundness of a surety for his client (Rule 10).

Duty to the Client (Section II; Rules 11-32 [VERIFY numbers]): an advocate is bound to accept any brief in the courts or tribunals or before any other authority in or before which he professes to practise at a fee consistent with his standing at the Bar and the nature of the case, subject to special circumstances justifying refusal (Rule 11); shall not ordinarily withdraw from engagements once accepted without sufficient cause and unless reasonable and sufficient notice is given to the client; he shall refund any part of the fee not earned (Rule 12); shall not accept a brief or appear in a case in which he has reason to believe that he will be a witness, and if he becomes a witness he shall not continue to appear except as to formal matters (Rule 13); shall, at the commencement of his engagement and during its progress, make full and frank disclosure to his client relating to his connection with the parties and any interest in or about the controversy as are likely to affect the client's judgment (Rule 14); shall uphold the interest of his client fearlessly by all fair and honourable means without regard to any unpleasant consequences to himself or any other; he shall defend a person accused of a crime regardless of his personal opinion as to the guilt of the accused (Rule 15 - the counsel's duty is to ensure fair trial); shall not act on the instructions of any person other than his client or his authorised agent (Rule 16); shall not do anything whereby he abuses or takes advantage of the confidence reposed in him by his client (Rule 24); shall not stipulate for a fee contingent on the results of litigation or agree to share the proceeds thereof (Rule 20); shall not buy or traffic in or stipulate for or agree to receive any share or interest in any actionable claim (Rule 21); shall not, directly or indirectly, bid for or purchase, either in his own name or in any other name, any property sold in execution of a decree in a proceeding in which he was professionally engaged (Rule 22); keep accounts of the client's money (Rules 26-27); shall not apply moneys received for expenses to fees and vice versa except with express instructions (Rule 27); after termination of the proceeding, is at liberty to appropriate towards the settled fee due to him any sum remaining with him out of the amount paid or sent for expenses (Rule 28) and, where the fee is unsettled, to deduct the fee payable under the Court rules and refund the balance (Rule 29); shall furnish a copy of accounts to the client on demand on payment of the cost (Rule 30); shall not enter into arrangements whereby funds in his hands are converted into loans (Rule 31); shall not lend money to his client for the purpose of any action or legal proceedings in which he is engaged (but may agree to advance court fees, expenses of witnesses and other disbursements) (Rule 32).

Duty to the opponent (Section III; Rules 33-34 [VERIFY]): an advocate shall not in any way communicate or negotiate or call upon the opposite party who is represented by an advocate except through that advocate; shall do his best to carry out all legitimate promises made to the opposite party even though not reduced to writing or enforceable under the rules of the court; shall not appear for the opposite party in a case where he previously advised or acted for the other party in connection with the same matter.

Duty to colleagues (Section IV; [VERIFY numbers]): an advocate shall not solicit work or advertise, either directly or indirectly, whether by circulars, advertisements, touts, personal communications, interviews not warranted by personal relations, furnishing or inspiring newspaper comments or producing his photographs to be published in connection with cases in which he has been engaged or concerned (Rule 36); his sign-board or nameplate should be of reasonable size and shall not indicate that he is or has been president or member of a Bar Council or Association, or that he has been Government Advocate, or that he is a specialist; shall not permit his professional services or his name to be used in aid of, or to make possible, the unauthorised practice of law by any law agency (Rule 37); shall not enter appearance in any case in which there is already another advocate engaged for the party except with the consent of such advocate (or, if consent is not produced, only after giving reasons) (Rule 38-ish); shall not accept a vakalatnama without the previous advocate's fee being cleared where the earlier engagement was for the same case unless it is shown that the party has paid or the advocate has been discharged [VERIFY]. The BCI relaxed the advertising bar in 2008 to allow advocates to provide information on websites (name, contact details, area of practice, qualifications) without soliciting.

Other employment (Section VII; Rules 47-52 [VERIFY]): an advocate shall not personally engage in any business; but he may be a sleeping partner in a firm doing business provided that, in the opinion of the Bar Council, the nature of the business is not inconsistent with the dignity of the profession (Rule 47); an advocate may be a Director or Chairman of the Board of Directors of a company with no objection if he does not practise as a Managing Director or Secretary (Rule 48); an advocate shall not be a full-time salaried employee of any person, Government, firm, corporation or concern so long as he continues to practise, and shall on taking up such employment intimate the fact to the Bar Council whose roll he is borne and shall thereupon cease to practise as an advocate so long as he continues in such employment (Rule 49); an advocate who is a Law Officer of the Central Government or of a State or of any public body or authority and is designated as such by the terms of his appointment and is required to act or plead in courts is exempted (Rule 50). Dr. Haniraj L. Chulani v. Bar Council of Maharashtra and Goa (1996): a person practising another profession (medicine) cannot simultaneously be enrolled; Sushma Suri v. Government (NCT of Delhi) (1999): a legal adviser or law officer who acts or pleads in courts may continue to practise; Satish Kumar Sharma v. Bar Council of H.P. (2001): a full-time salaried employee cannot practise.

Fees: the fee is a matter of agreement; a contingent fee is prohibited (champerty) (Rule 20); advocates cannot claim a share in the decretal amount; a fee agreement must not be unconscionable; an advocate cannot demand fees from a client without rendering service; non-payment does not allow withholding of papers (R.D. Saxena). Retainer; refund of unearned fee (Rule 12). The Supreme Court in Re: Fees (V.C. Rangadurai) and in has said that the bar should not become a trade.

Senior advocates (Part VI Chapter I): a senior advocate shall not (a) file a vakalatnama or act in any court, tribunal or before any person or authority mentioned in s.30; (b) appear without an Advocate-on-Record in the Supreme Court or without another advocate in other courts (rules for 'junior'); (c) accept instructions to appear except from an advocate; (d) accept directly from a client any brief to appear or draft pleadings; he may, however, advise on legal questions or settle drafts; he shall not do conveyancing, drafting of pleadings or affidavits (the 2023 BCI amendments relaxed these in some respects [VERIFY]); a senior advocate in the Supreme Court must have a prescribed 'practice' and can be designated by the Court under s.16.

Dress (Part VI, Chapter IV): advocates appearing in the Supreme Court, High Courts, subordinate courts, tribunals and authorities: black buttoned-up coat, chapkan, achkan, black sherwani and white bands with advocates' gown; women advocates - black and full-sleeve jacket or blouse, white collar-band, saree or long skirt or churidar-kurta or salwar-kameez or traditional dress in white or black or any subdued colour; bands and gowns not to be worn in public places except courts and ceremonial occasions; advocates in summer may wear white shirt or blouse with bands (without the coat) in subordinate courts. (Regulation under s.49(1)(gg).) Neckties/ bands: rule of dress is not tested beyond these basics.

Additional duties: legal aid and pro bono (Art 39A; Legal Services Authorities Act); duty to maintain the dignity of the profession; duty not to misrepresent the court; duty to disclose adverse authority and to assist the court; duty to keep client secrets (BSA s.132 - see 9.E4); duty not to disclose; duty of fairness to witnesses; duty not to coach or tamper with witnesses (misconduct under BNS ss.229-232); duty not to engage in sexual misconduct or harassment (POSH Act extends to Bar associations).

key_provisions.content: No contingent fee; no sharing of proceeds.

mnemonics: Duties: 'C-C-O-C' - Court, Client, Opponent, Colleagues. Prohibitions: contingent fee (20), actionable claims (21), purchase at execution sale (22), advertising (36), business (47).

sections.title: Contempt of Court, Strikes, Professional Privilege (BSA ss.132-134), Legal Aid, Duties as Officer of the Court and Recent Rulings (2024-2026)
sections.articles: Contempt of Courts Act 1971; Arts 129, 215; BSA ss.132-134 (Evidence Act ss.126-129); Advocates Act ss.35, 49; Consumer Protection Act
sections.overview: Ethics overlaps with contempt law, privilege and strike jurisprudence. Includes the October 2025 Supreme Court ruling on summoning advocates.
must_know: Contempt of Courts Act 1971 - definitions (s.2): 'civil contempt' - wilful disobedience to any judgment, decree, direction, order, writ or other process of a court or wilful breach of an undertaking given to a court; 'criminal contempt' - publication (words spoken or written, signs, visible representations) which (i) scandalises or tends to scandalise, or lowers or tends to lower the authority of any court; (ii) prejudices or interferes or tends to interfere with the due course of any judicial proceeding; or (iii) interferes or tends to interfere with, or obstructs or tends to obstruct, the administration of justice in any other manner. Defences: innocent publication and distribution (s.3); fair and accurate report of judicial proceedings (s.4); fair criticism of a judicial act after the case is finally decided (s.5); complaint against presiding officers of subordinate courts made in good faith to a superior court (s.6); publication of proceedings in chambers or in camera (s.7); other defences (s.8); truth as a defence if justified in public interest and the request is bona fide (s.13(b), inserted by the 2006 Amendment). s.12 - punishment: simple imprisonment for a term up to six months, or fine up to Rs 2,000, or both; the accused may be discharged or the punishment remitted on apology if the court is satisfied that the apology is bona fide; the court may withhold punishment if the contempt does not substantially interfere with the administration of justice (s.13(a)). s.14 - procedure where contempt is in the face of the Supreme Court or a High Court; s.15 - cognisance of criminal contempt (other than in the face of the court) by the Supreme Court or High Court on its own motion or on a motion by the Attorney-General/Solicitor-General (Supreme Court), Advocate-General (High Court) or any other person with the written consent of the Attorney-General/Advocate-General; s.17 - procedure after cognisance (notice, hearing, affidavit); s.19 - appeal as of right to the Supreme Court from an order punishing for contempt (within 30 days); s.20 - limitation: no court shall initiate any proceeding for contempt after the expiry of one year from the date on which the contempt is alleged to have been committed. Constitutional contempt power: Art 129 (Supreme Court as a court of record), Art 215 (High Courts). Cases: Re: Prashant Bhushan (2020) - fine of Re 1 (tweets); Baradakanta Mishra v. Registrar of Orissa High Court (1974) - scandalising; E.M. Sankaran Namboodiripad v. T. Narayanan Nambiar (1970); Perspective Publications v. State of Maharashtra (1969); In re: Arundhati Roy (2002); Dr. D.C. Saxena v. Hon'ble the Chief Justice of India (1996); Re: Vijay Kurle (2020) - advocates who made allegations against judges were held guilty of contempt.

Advocates and contempt: an advocate is an officer of the court; the judge-advocate relationship rests on mutual respect (BCI Rule 2-3); remarks against judges outside court may amount to contempt; the High Court may take action; the Bar Council's disciplinary power is independent (Pravin C. Shah; Vinay Chandra Mishra). Court's power to censure advocates, withdraw their pre-audience, restrain from appearing: Bar Council of India v. High Court of Kerala (2004). Remarks in court against the judge by an advocate are grounds for contempt and misconduct (M.B. Sanghi).

Strikes by lawyers: Ex-Capt. Harish Uppal v. Union of India (2002/2003) - lawyers have no right to go on strike or give a call for boycott of courts, not even on a token strike; protests may be held by press statements, TV interviews, black or white armbands, and peaceful demonstration outside and away from court premises, not affecting court proceedings; any lawyer who abstains from work in breach of this is liable for professional misconduct and the Bar Council must take action; the courts may impose costs on the lawyers who strike (Ramon Services Pvt. Ltd. v. Subhash Kapoor, 2001 - a client may recover compensation from advocate who abstains); Common Cause v. Union of India (2006); Krishnakant Tamrakar v. State of M.P. (2018) - strike by lawyers is illegal; the High Courts to take cognisance; Bar Council of India's Rule 'no strike' (BCI Resolution); the Court said that the BCI must act against defaulters.

Advocate-client privilege: Evidence Act ss.126-129 now BSA ss.132-134: s.132 BSA (s.126 Evidence Act): no advocate shall at any time be permitted, unless with his client's express consent, to disclose any communication made to him in the course and for the purpose of his employment as such advocate by or on behalf of his client, or to state the contents or condition of any document with which he has become acquainted in the course and for the purpose of his professional employment, or to disclose any advice given by him to his client in the course and for the purpose of such employment; exceptions: (1) any such communication made in furtherance of any illegal purpose; (2) any fact observed by any advocate in the course of his employment showing that any crime or fraud has been committed since the commencement of his employment; the obligation continues after the employment has ceased. s.133 BSA (s.127): same protection for interpreters, clerks and servants of advocates; s.134 BSA (s.129): no one shall be compelled to disclose to the court any confidential communication between himself and his legal professional adviser unless he offers himself as a witness (then only as necessary). Waiver: privilege is the client's, not the advocate's; privilege is not waived merely by the client giving evidence.

In re: Summoning Advocates who give legal opinion or represent parties during investigation of cases and related issues (31 October 2025; 2025 INSC 1275; suo motu proceedings after the Enforcement Directorate's summons to a senior advocate): the Supreme Court held that investigating agencies and police cannot summon advocates to disclose the legal advice given to clients or to disclose communications with clients, except within the exceptions of s.132 BSA (illegal purpose/crime or fraud); any summons to an advocate must have the prior written approval of a superior officer (not below the rank of Superintendent of Police) recording reasons that the case falls within the exceptions; the advocate may challenge the summons before the court under s.528 BNSS or Art 226; production of digital devices of the advocate can be ordered only by a court (not by the investigating officer), and the advocate has the right to have the privilege decided by a judicial forum; the Court clarified that in-house counsel employed full-time by a company are not 'advocates' for the purposes of s.132 BSA (their communication with the employer is not protected by that section, though s.134 BSA - the protection for confidential communications with a legal adviser - may apply in respect of communications to the company's legal advisers) [VERIFY details]. This decision was followed by the observations that legal professional privilege is a facet of the right to a fair trial (Art 21).

Legal aid and public duty: advocates are expected to provide legal aid to the poor as part of their obligation (BCI Rules; Legal Services Authorities Act); State-paid legal aid advocates; duty of counsel to defend an accused (Rule 15); Mohammed Ajmal Mohammad Amir Kasab v. State of Maharashtra (2012) - duty of the Court to appoint a competent lawyer; Khatri; Suk Das. Lawyers' duty not to refuse a brief because the client is unpopular (A.S. Mohammed Rafi).

Consumer Protection and advocates: Bar of Indian Lawyers (through its President Jasbir Singh Malik) v. D.K. Gandhi PS Rao, Deputy Director, National Institute of Communicable Diseases (2024): the Supreme Court held (May 2024) that the legal profession is sui generis; advocates' services are not 'service' under s.2(42) of the Consumer Protection Act 2019 (and corresponding provisions of the 1986 Act); the NCDRC decision in Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha line did not apply; consumer fora cannot entertain complaints on deficiency in services of advocates; remedies lie in disciplinary proceedings or a civil suit for professional negligence [VERIFY]. Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab (2005) - professional negligence standard.

Other ethical/ regulatory developments: BCI's Rules on advocates' welfare; Advocates' Welfare Fund; BCI's decisions on non-practising advocates and on the AIBE; BCI's resolutions on the conduct of Bar elections; the Bar Council of India (Verification) Rules 2015; Law Commission 266th report; the Government's Advocates (Amendment) Bill 2025 draft (withdrawn) [VERIFY]; the Bar Council elections and the cap on tenure; use of AI and ethical standards (BCI and High Courts have issued advisories on AI-generated pleadings and citation of non-existent precedents - misconduct if filed carelessly) [VERIFY]; social-media advertising and the BCI's 2008 resolution.

Advocate-client privilege; exceptions: illegal purpose; crime or fraud after employment.

BSA 132-134 = Evidence Act 126-129.
